summary: Describes the Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol, a cryptographically strong network authentication and key exchange mechanism based on a password. The password itself is not sent over the network.

eli5.summary: You and a server both prove you know a secret without ever saying it out loud, and end up sharing a new secret for talking.

questions: how does secure remote password work
does srp send the password over the network
subtitle: Prove you know a password to a server without ever sending it, and end up with a shared session key.

tldr.problem: Passwords sent in the clear can be sniffed, and even challenge-response schemes let an attacker with captured traffic test guessed passwords against a dictionary. Many systems also have to keep their password database secret.
tldr.mechanism: The host stores a salt and a verifier computed from the password. Client and host each send one Diffie-Hellman-style value, derive the same session key, and then exchange hash proofs that the keys match.
tldr.outcome: The password never crosses the network, a captured exchange cannot be used to check guesses, and both sides get a key for privacy or integrity protection. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 2945 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text describes an abstract protocol rather than a message format for any one application.

sections.title: Why Passwords Need Better Protection
sections.content:
RFC 2945 describes the Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol. The RFC opens with a two-sided problem: users like passwords they can remember, but most password systems offer little protection even against passive attackers when the passwords are weak.

Sending a password in the clear is easy to eavesdrop on. Challenge-response schemes such as those in RFC 2095 and RFC 1760 defeat simple sniffing, but they can still fall to a dictionary attack: the attacker captures a legitimate run of the protocol and uses it to check guessed passwords from a precompiled list.

The RFC also objects to systems that must keep the host's password file secret because it holds the password P or a private hash h(P). SRP is said to meet the strictest requirements of RFC 1704 for a non-disclosing authentication protocol, using a single Diffie-Hellman-style round of computation.
sections.eli5: If you shout your password across a crowded room, anyone can hear it. SRP lets you prove you know it without saying it, so listeners learn nothing they can use.

sections.title: Scope and the Integer Mapping
sections.content:
The document describes an abstract protocol, sometimes called "SRP-3" for historical reasons. It does not fit SRP to any particular Internet protocol, and it leaves the exact message format, including padding, to the implementor.

The one thing it does specify is how to turn byte strings into integers, because Internet protocols are byte-oriented while SRP does algebra. An n-byte string is read as a base 256 number with the most significant byte first. When converting back, the first byte must be non-zero. If padding is needed, the RFC recommends adding zero bytes at the start, since converting back discards leading zeros.

Wherever the text says SHA, it means SHA-1.
sections.eli5: Computers send bytes, but the math needs numbers. This section just says how to read a row of bytes as one big number, and everyone must read it the same way.

sections.title: What the Host Stores
sections.content:
The host keeps, for each user, a triplet: the username, a password verifier and a salt. An entry is made by picking a random salt, computing x = SHA(salt | SHA(username | ":" | raw password)), and storing v = g^x % N as the verifier.

The raw password and x are not stored. The 160-bit SHA output is implicitly converted to an integer before it is used. The RFC notes that a leaked password database still forces an attacker into an expensive dictionary search.
sections.eli5: Instead of keeping your password in a drawer, the server keeps a scrambled fingerprint of it plus a random pinch of extra spice. The fingerprint is no use for logging in.

sections.title: The Exchange
sections.content:
The client starts by sending its username U, and the host answers with the stored salt s. The client picks a random a and sends A = g^a % N. The host picks a random b and replies with B = (v + g^b) % N.

The client recomputes x from the salt and the password the user types. Both sides then compute the same value S (by two different formulas) and turn it into the session key K = SHA_Interleave(S). The parameter u is a 32-bit unsigned integer taken from the first 32 bits of the SHA-1 hash of B, most significant bit first.

Two aborts are mandatory: the client MUST abort if B % N is zero, and the host MUST abort if A % N is zero. The host MUST send B only after receiving A.

To finish, each side proves it holds the same K. The client sends M = H(H(N) XOR H(g) | H(U) | s | A | B | K). The server checks it, and if it does not match the server MUST abort and signal an error before answering the client's challenge, because answering could compromise the user's password. If it matches, the server MUST respond with H(A | M | K), which the client verifies.

These steps need not map one to one onto real messages. The RFC shows a consolidated form: the client sends U and A together, and the host replies with s and B together.
sections.eli5: Each side whispers a scrambled number to the other. With a little math they both end up with the same secret key. Then they each show a stamp made from that key, and if the stamps match, they know the other side had the right password.

sections.title: Interleaved SHA
sections.content:
SRP-SHA1 makes a session key twice as long as one SHA-1 output using SHA_Interleave. Remove all leading zero bytes from the input. If the remaining length is odd, also remove the first byte. Call the result T.

Put the even-numbered bytes of T into a string E and the odd-numbered bytes into F. Hash each with SHA-1 to get G and H, then interleave the two hashes as G[0] | H[0] | G[1] | H[1] | ... | G[19] | H[19]. The result is 40 bytes (320 bits) long.
sections.eli5: Deal the bytes like cards into two piles, scramble each pile separately, then shuffle the piles back together. The result is a longer, stronger key.

sections.title: Group Parameters and Other Hashes
sections.content:
The values N and g must be agreed by both parties. They can be set in advance, or the host can send them in the first message along with the salt. For maximum security, N should be a safe prime (N = 2q + 1 with q also prime), and g should be a generator modulo N.

SRP can use hash functions other than SHA. If the output length differs from SHA's 20 bytes, some message lengths change but the operation does not. Earlier versions used MD5 (RFC 1321). Keyed hashes such as HMAC (RFC 2104) are also recommended, using K to key the hash instead of concatenating it with other parameters. Any hash used should produce at least 16 bytes of output and change in a significant nonlinear way when the input changes slightly.
sections.eli5: Both sides need to agree on the same big number and rulebook before they start, like picking the same game board. You can also swap in a different scrambler as long as it is strong enough.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says SRP removes the need to send cleartext passwords and, through its key exchange, enables encryption. It is designed to resist not just casual sniffing but an attacker with a password dictionary working from captured traffic, and it resists active network attacks as well.

The private values a and b behave like Diffie-Hellman private values and have similar length and entropy needs. Implementations may lengthen u if both sides agree, but it is not recommended to make it shorter than 32 bits.

If the host's password database were revealed, an attacker would still need an expensive dictionary search, since checking a guess needs an exponentiation. Hosts are still advised to protect their password files.
sections.eli5: Even if a burglar copies the server's list, it is only scrambled fingerprints, and testing each guess takes real work. The server should still lock the list away.
